common_name: Mrs. George H. Pring Water Lily

planting.note: Set the tuber in a submerged container once pond water is reliably above 70F, since this tropical lily stalls in cold water.

directions: Introduced by George Pring at the Missouri Botanical Garden and named for his wife, this night-blooming tropical lily opens large, star-shaped, creamy white flowers with faint gray-green stripes through the petals and sepals, usually unfurling several at once on tall stems above the mottled purple-blotched pads. Expect the fragrant blooms to open at dusk and stay open into the following morning, making it a good choice for a patio pond enjoyed in the evening. Plant the tuber in a wide container of heavy aquatic soil and keep it in full sun with water that stays warm all season, feeding monthly with aquatic fertilizer tablets. Where winters are cold, lift and store the dormant tuber in damp sand indoors rather than leaving it in the pond.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

planting.note: Plant once water stays warm; this smaller tropical lily suits tub gardens and small to large ponds alike.

directions: Bred by George Pring in 1956 and later honored with the Henry Shaw Gold Medal, this compact tropical day-blooming lily carries bright lemon-yellow, star-shaped flowers with a light fragrance over olive-green pads marked with maroon mottling. It is one of the more floriferous yellow tropicals, opening daily through the warm months and tolerating slightly less sun than many other day bloomers. Grow it in a generously sized container of heavy garden soil set in full sun once water temperatures are consistently warm, and feed regularly to keep up the flower count. In climates with cold winters, bring the tuber indoors before frost and store it moist and cool until the following spring.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Best in a medium to large pond where its heavily mottled leaves have room to spread.

directions: Raised by hybridizer Martin Randig, this tropical day-blooming lily is prized for its deep raspberry-pink, star-shaped flowers and strikingly variegated leaves, which are heavily blotched purple on top and red-spotted beneath. The 7 to 9 inch blooms carry a light fragrance and open reliably through the growing season on a vigorous, free-flowering plant. Site the tuber in a wide planting container in full sun with 6 to 12 inches of water over the crown once temperatures are reliably warm. Divide crowded tubers every couple of years and overwinter them indoors in frost-prone regions, since this cultivar has no cold tolerance.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

planting.note: Tolerates a bit more shade than most tropical lilies, but still flowers best with a full sun pond site.

directions: This tropical day-blooming lily opens fragrant, cup-shaped flowers that shift through coppery pink, yellow, and orange tones above large, heavily mottled pads, giving each bloom a changeable, sunset-like look. It is a notably vigorous grower that can spread wider than many other tropical cultivars, so it suits medium to large ponds better than small tubs. Unlike most tropical lilies it will still produce a respectable show with as little as four hours of direct sun, though full sun brings the heaviest bloom. Keep the tuber in warm water through summer and move it to a protected indoor location before the first frost, since it has no hardiness once temperatures drop.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Give this large grower a pond at least 5 feet across so the giant pads and flowers have room.

directions: Hybridized by George Pring in 1949 and named for a water lily specialist at Kew Gardens, this tropical day-blooming lily produces some of the largest flowers in the genus, with sky-blue petals surrounding bright yellow stamens on blooms that can exceed a foot across. The sweetly fragrant flowers open mid-morning and stay open until dusk during the height of summer, making it a long-lasting daily show. Because of its size it is best suited to medium or large ponds with at least four to five hours of direct sun. Plant the tuber in a large container of heavy soil once the water is warm, and bring it indoors or treat it as an annual where winters bring hard frost.

planting.note: Set the rhizome in a planting crate in 6 to 30 inches of water once the pond has thawed and warmed.

directions: Developed by hybridizer Perry D. Slocum in 1990, this hardy water lily carries fully double, snow-white, star-shaped flowers four to six inches across over smooth, round green pads. It blooms heavily from early summer well into autumn, outlasting many single-flowered hardy cultivars. Plant the rhizome horizontally in a two-gallon or larger crate of heavy garden soil topped with pea gravel, and set it where it gets at least six hours of direct sun. Because it is fully hardy, the crate can overwinter at the bottom of the pond below the ice line in most regions, with division needed only every few years as the crown becomes crowded.

planting.note: Despite the sunset-colored bloom, this is a tender tropical cultivar and cannot stay in a pond that freezes.

directions: This tropical day-blooming lily earns its name from cup-shaped flowers that blend pink, orange, and yellow in a single bloom, with the deepest pink color at the petal tips fading toward yellow near the center. The fragrant flowers open over deep green, pink-overcast foliage and keep coming in flushes through the warm months on a free-flowering plant. It performs best with eight or more hours of direct sun and warm, nutrient-rich water. Plant the tuber in a wide container once temperatures are reliably warm, and either grow it as a warm-season annual or lift and store the dormant tuber indoors before frost in colder climates.

planting.note: A vigorous spreader best given a full square meter or more of open water surface to fill.

directions: Raised by the hybridizer Thomas in 1962, this large hardy water lily produces pointed, pure white petals that deepen to light yellow toward the center, opening above broad green pads up to eight inches across. It is a vigorous, free-flowering cultivar well suited to covering open water in a medium to large pond. Plant the rhizome in a generous crate of heavy soil in full sun at a depth of 8 to 24 inches and feed through the growing season for the best flower count. Being fully hardy, the planting crate can simply be lowered to the bottom of the pond for winter in most temperate climates, with repotting needed only every few years.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: A large, vigorous hardy lily that needs a sizeable pond to show off its giant blooms.

directions: One of the oldest hardy lily cultivars still in commerce, this Latour-Marliac introduction opens giant, canary-yellow, star-shaped flowers up to nine inches across with narrow petals that curve slightly inward. The blooms rise well above the water on strong stems and stay open later into the afternoon than many other hardy yellows, set against dark green, lightly spotted pads. It grows vigorously, so give it a medium to large pond where it can spread four to six feet without crowding neighboring lilies. Plant the rhizome in a crate of heavy soil in full sun, repot every two to three years as the crown fills in, and feed regularly through the warm season for the best flower display.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: A true miniature suited to tubs and small pools; avoid pairing with vigorous large-pad cultivars that would shade it out.

directions: Bred by Dr. Kirk Strawn in 1993, this miniature hardy lily carries fully double, ivory-white flowers barely three inches across that are tinged soft pink and centered with bright golden stamens, held just above small apple-green pads. Its tiny stature and shallow water needs make it one of the best hardy lilies for a half-barrel water garden or small container pool where a full-sized cultivar would be out of scale. Plant the small rhizome in a modest pot of heavy soil in only 6 to 20 inches of water and full sun, and expect the floating mat of foliage to stay compact. Because it is fully hardy, the pot can overwinter at pond bottom in most climates, though container water gardens should be moved somewhere protected from a hard freeze.

planting.note: A large, long-blooming cultivar best suited to medium or large ponds in full sun.

directions: Bred by George Pring in 1917, this tropical day-blooming lily produces gigantic, light blue to lavender flowers with bright yellow stamens and a delicate fragrance over striking mottled leaves. It is noted for opening unusually early in the day and staying open later than most other day bloomers, giving a longer daily viewing window than typical tropical lilies. A single well-established plant can send up six or more open flowers at once. Grow the tuber in a large container of heavy soil in full sun and warm water, feeding regularly through summer, and either treat it as an annual or overwinter the dormant tuber indoors where winters bring freezing water.

planting.note: Start a new tuber under just a few inches of water and gradually raise the water level as leaves rise above the surface.

directions: Hybridized by Perry D. Slocum, this large lotus opens warm pink flowers with just a hint of orange that can reach up to a foot across, held well above the water on tall, sturdy stems alongside large blue-green leaves. It is a dependable, vigorous grower that returns reliably each year once established, making it a favorite among lotus growers despite its considerable size. Plant the tuber horizontally just below the soil surface in a wide, heavy container, starting it in only a couple of inches of water before raising the depth to 12 to 24 inches over the crown as aerial leaves develop. Give it full sun and a season or two to settle in, after which it can be left undisturbed for several years before dividing becomes necessary.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

planting.note: More shade-tolerant than full-size papyrus, but keep it sheltered from strong wind, which can snap the slender stems.

directions: Discovered in 1993 during propagation research at Kagawa University in Japan, this compact sport of Egyptian papyrus grows only two to three feet tall instead of the ten-plus feet of the wild species, while still producing the same tufted umbels of thread-like bracts topped with tiny brown flower clusters. Its small scale and tolerance of light shade make it a practical choice for container water gardens and smaller ponds where full-sized papyrus would overwhelm the space. Plant divisions in heavy soil at the pond margin or in a submerged pot up to about a foot deep, keeping the crown consistently wet to wholly submerged through the growing season. It has no frost tolerance, so gardeners outside the tropics should grow it as a container specimen brought indoors, or a warm-season annual, before the first freeze.
